full_title: Risk of Mission Impacts and Long-Term Health Issues due to Decompression Sickness
risk_statement: Given that decompression sickness (DCS) is a potential risk for every spaceflight/mission (e.g., EVA or cabin depressurization) and must be mitigated to acceptable risk levels; limitations in quantitative understanding of DCS will lead to conservative DCS risk mitigation countermeasures with significant operational, engineering, and/or secondary health/performance impacts. HSRB State of Knowledge As of today, no reported cases of DCS during flight, yet ground studies with similar decompression stress do cause DCS. Ground studies stop at first symptoms of DCS, so little is known on the progression of DCS symptoms. NASA standards exist for both DCS prevention and treatment and are being incorporated into new programs. Effects of fractional gravity on DCS risk are currently unknown, but will increase the risk compared to microgravity. Current operational pre-breathe (PB) protocols are validated only for the microgravity environment and require hours of PB including multiple procedural steps requiring ground and intravehicular (IV) support to facilitate timing and order of airlock and suit preparation operations. Countermeasure Development: Based on a successful staged decompression to a 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 atmosphere developed for shuttle EVA to reduce prep. time. The 8.2 psia / 34% O2 environment with variable pressure space suit is the recommended approach and is being validated to support an efficient and flexible EVA architecture, however, the ability to implement the Exploration Atmosphere as recommended may be affected by factors including: schedule & budgetary constraints, contract mechanisms, international partnerships, personnel changes, cross-program dependencies, and unanticipated technical challenges. Ability to accurately inform major cross-program architectural decisions is limited by significant uncertainty in unvalidated DCS risk estimation tools. Mitigation Strategy Research tasks associated with understanding, quantifying, and mitigating the risk of DCS during spaceflight are described in the EVA Risk Strategy ( https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/risk.aspx?i=84 ).
nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Decompression Sickness
When astronauts move from a pressurized environment like a spacecraft to the lower-pressure environment encountered during spacewalks, health complications can arise due to what’s known as decompression sickness. During decompression sickness, dissolved nitrogen in the bloodstream begins to bubble, which can damage body tissues.
Also known as “the bends,” decompression sickness can occur on Earth when scuba divers attempt to surface too fast. As they quickly ascend, nitrogen gas dissolved in their body tissues rapidly forms bubbles which can cause pain so severe it may force a diver to double over. In severe cases, these bubbles can impact breathing or even block blood vessels and cause stroke-like symptoms.
In space, this same phenomenon can occur when an astronaut moves from a spacecraft to a lower-pressure spacesuit for spacewalks. Spacewalks are one of the highest-risk activities an astronaut will ever do, so decompression sickness is both a health and operational risk.
Earth-based training in both high- and low-pressure environments prior to missions helps astronauts know what to expect in altered pressure situations, including when they might be at risk for decompression sickness. Current protocols hold that when experiencing decompression sickness symptoms, astronauts should safely but rapidly end their spacewalk and return to the pressurized environment of their spacecraft.
Future missions deeper into space will likely require more frequent spacewalks. NASA is preparing for associated risks in a variety of ways. For instance, new variable pressure space suits currently in development may provide some initial ways to address decompression sickness during the spacewalk itself. The suits’ technology aims to allow astronauts to quickly increase the pressure within their suits, which could help stabilize the afflicted crew member and allow for safer return. But astronauts who wear such suits may also experience reduced mobility, decreased manual dexterity, and increased fatigue during spacewalks – since pressurized suits are heavier – so decisions will need to be made about risk tradeoffs.
In addition, the spacecraft for future deep space missions could be designed to operate at lower pressures, helping to limit the pressure changes between habitat and spacesuit, which will reduce risks. full_title: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Hypoxia
risk_statement: Given that future human exploration missions require robust, flexible Extravehicular Activity (EVA) architecture protocols that include the use of a reduced pressure cabin atmosphere enabling staged denitrogenation, there is a possibility that this atmosphere could result in compromised health and performance to the crewmember due to exposure to mild hypobaric hypoxia. Notes: - In addition to hypobaric hypoxia associated with staged denitrogenation, there are additional factors that can result in hypoxic exposure to the crewmember such as cabin depressurization, Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) failure, toxic exposure or crewmember illness/injury. - Planned research and countermeasures will focus on mild hypoxia associated with hypoxia related to staged denitrogenation. HSRB State of Knowledge The exploration atmosphere (8.2 psia/34% O2) was selected by the Exploration Atmospheres Working Group (EAWG) because it was considered to be a mildly hypoxic atmosphere with acceptable flammability risk and low O2 prebreathe (PB) overhead to maintain acceptable DCS risk while facilitating efficient EVA operations. The 8.2/34 environment (PI O2 = 128 mmHg) is physiologically similar in terms of O2 availability to the nominal shuttle and ISS staged decompression atmosphere of 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 (PI O2 = 127 mmHg). Both environments provide a hypoxic dose as modeled between 4000-8300 ft altitude. The staged decompression was used on 40 different shuttle missions for durations of 1 to 8 days. Of most concern are the potential effects on the increased intracranial pressure, visual impairment, cognitive performance, sensorimotor dysfunction, oxidative damage and sleep quality. Other areas of focus include incidence and treatment of acute mountain sickness (AMS), development of new exercise countermeasure protocols and effective food preparation at 8.2 psia. Per HLS requirements, the original 7-day limit in NASA-STD-3001 for mildly hypoxic environments was extended to 30 days with monitoring because it was shown to improve the net risk posture for flight crew health and performance. With an agreement on what monitoring is required, this 30-day duration could be extended to indefinite with monitoring for all missions other than Mars, which will need additional assessment due to the long transit in microgravity prior to use of staged denitrogenation environments. Mitigation Strategy Research tasks to investigate physiological responses and mitigating hypoxia risk associated with exposure to hypobaric hypoxic stress as an exploration atmosphere and cycling between mild hypoxia and mild hyperoxia during EVAs is captured under the EVA Risk Strategy ( https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/risk.aspx?i=84 ).
nasa_ref_summary:
Future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond will require more frequent spacewalks. But keeping astronauts safe and healthy during any spacewalk currently requires many hours of preparation and a large supply of pure oxygen. Astronauts must inhale pure oxygen over several hours prior to spacewalks to avoid decompression sickness, also known as “the bends.”
To help slash the pure oxygen needs for future frequent spacewalks, NASA’s spacecraft for deep-space missions will have astronauts live and work in a constant partial cabin depressurization (something that now only occurs in the airlock prior to spacewalks). This altered cabin environment will help reduce nitrogen in the body passively.
Yet that partial depressurization will simultaneously increase the risk of mild hypoxia — a condition that occurs when oxygen levels in body tissues become lower than normal. Mild hypoxia, if untreated, can cause confusion, headaches, vision impairment, and trouble sleeping.
NASA’s health experts are researching hypoxia to design protocols that balance oxygen concentration and pressure to optimize astronaut health and performance before and during spacewalks. Creating spacesuits that have the option for crews to be able to toggle pressure increases inside their suits while conducting spacewalks is another area of current research.
No current ground-based study exists to test different oxygen exposure levels on humans while they’re experiencing all the stressors of spaceflight. Instead, scientists are using decades of archived health data on spacewalks to try to extrapolate answers to several questions. For example, will a mildly hypoxic, reduced-pressure environment make any known astronaut health issues worse? If so, what oxygen levels might be tolerable? Scientists are also gathering data from studies conducted in pressure chambers that can simulate spaceflight atmospheres. Studying volunteers that spend hours or days in these chambers allows scientists to learn more about hypoxia and decompression sickness risks and to test potential interventions.
Researchers are using all these areas of research to build new health monitoring protocols and treatment strategies to track how future astronauts will adapt to partial depressurization. These new protocols are being incorporated into medical operations and planning for future missions.

full_title: Risk of Adverse Mission Outcomes Due to Earth Independent Human-Systems Operations
risk_statement: Given decreasing real-time ground support for execution of Earth independent critical, complex operations during future exploration missions, there is a possibility of adverse performance outcomes, most consequentially that crew are unable to adequately respond to unanticipated critical malfunctions or execute safety-critical procedures. HSRB State of Knowledge Critical malfunctions requiring Crew/Mission Control Center (MCC) management occurred at a rate of 1.7 times per year for International Space Station (ISS) averaged over the lifetime and 3-4 times per year in the burn in phase for the vehicle. These averages do not include EVA data, which greatly increases the incident rate. Prior experience from the Apollo program showed 10/11 crewed missions experienced significant anomalies where crew relied heavily on MCC expertise in real-time. These failure patterns are in line with those observed in other complex engineered systems (e.g., oil rigs, launch systems, commercial aviation, etc.). Mitigation Strategy The Human Systems Integration Architecture (HSIA) risk is comprised of an integrated representation of the Human Factors risk areas of vehicle design and habitability, human computer interaction, human automation and robotics integration, training, and task design. Future deep space missions will present new challenges for crew, and increased risks to human performance due to the stress, fatigue, radiation exposure, and isolation that characterizes these missions. In addition, crew will no longer be able to depend on real-time support from Mission Control due to distance from the Earth, but will have to work increasingly autonomously, performing critical tasks that were previously carried out by Flight Controllers. This greater crew/vehicle autonomy will depend, in part on advanced, on-board automated systems but also on new approaches to training, teaming and crew selection. Most importantly, it will depend on a successful integration of intelligent vehicle capabilities with crew capabilities. Ground laboratories, analogs, and the International Space Station (ISS) are utilized to answer research questions necessary to ensure that future Exploration crewmembers, who will be dealing with many unknowns, communication delays, and increasing autonomy, will be able to adequately perform their tasks and complete their missions. The HSIA risk provides a conceptual framework proposed to address the integration of onboard capability and crew roles and responsibilities necessary to enable crew to respond effectively and efficiently in the required increasing autonomous mission operations framework. Enabling a flight crew of 4 to perform the job that has traditionally been done by a ground crew of 40+ will require a fundamental rethinking of crew-vehicle integration and operations as well as crew-ground collaboration. A flight crew of 4 will need to function more autonomously in response to anticipated reduction in communication quantity and quality as well as unanticipated blackouts instead of depending on frequent real-time communications with a large Mission Control Center (MCC) ground support team of diverse specialties to provide directions (see Dempsey et al., 2018 for a detailed description of the range of support MCC provides). As outlined by Vera and Wu (2018), the impact will be felt particularly in dealing with unanticipated, off-nominal situations. Our current operational models therefore (tied to ground control) must evolve as mission operations become increasingly earth independent. Decreasing real-time ground support for the execution of complex operations during future exploration missions will require the flight crew to respond to potentially safety-critical anomalies with no established procedures on their own. A delay or absence of ground support during unanticipated contingencies can become a significant hazard and increase the risk of jeopardizing crew and vehicle safety if there are not sufficient onboard capabilities to assist with troubleshooting and contingency management. The attainment of increased crew autonomy therefore lies in the ability to complement and enhance crew capabilities so that the 4-person flight crew can, on their own, perform the kind of anomaly response that had previously been done mostly by MCC, and complete these activities in the face of the expected communication delays or unexpected blackouts. It is important to highlight that complex, engineered systems, automated/autonomous or not, will experience unanticipated safety critical malfunctions. These can be due, in part or in whole, to human error and/or space environment impacts, but can also be independent of these. Humans are the critical problem-solving components of complex engineered systems and while Artificial Intelligence, Intelligent/Autonomous Systems can help the human decision maker, especially with pattern analysis, the AI systems will not be able to provide actual problem-solving. Furthermore, reducing the number of crew in any system has the potential to raise risks of non-optimal Human System Integration in unanticipated ways. It is therefore critical that c apabilities be wrapped around the human(s) in order for safety critical issues to be addressable. To further mitigate the risk, specific factors have been identified (e.g., autonomy, anomaly detection and response, etc.) as highly relevant to long duration space missions. Thus, these gaps will focus specifically on understanding the true impact of these factors on long duration missions. At the conclusion of each task, the final report is reviewed and the relevant evidence report is modified or updated to indicate how the results of the research or technology activity address the gaps and contribute to quantifying or mitigating risk or risks. If applicable, the results will also be incorporated into NASA-STD-3001, VOL. II and the Human Integration Design Handbook (HIDH). Evaluations of countermeasure strategies will be made available in the evidence base and recommendations specific to countermeasure implementation for future missions, will also be defined.
nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support
NASA’s Mission Control Center trains astronauts to operate various systems on the International Space Station, including ultrasound and computer-based equipment. However, crews still rely on real-time assistance when problems arise. During longer and more distant missions from Earth, crew members will need more extensive training to know how to identify and fix any issues with systems, software, and equipment without real-time support from mission control.
NASA technologists strive to design user-friendly spaceflight systems so that astronauts can perform tasks independently, as needed. Crew members also receive training before a mission to familiarize themselves with various systems and respond to emergencies themselves. NASA researchers continue to work with industry partners and other experts to make spaceflight systems and vehicles easier to operate.
NASA astronauts train, on average, 300 hours in simulators before launch to help familiarize themselves with space vehicles and systems.

full_title: Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to Inadequate Food and Nutrition
risk_statement: Given that there is a constrained ability to supply adequate food in spaceflight missions, there is a possibility that inadequate nutrition will result in performance decrement, crew illness, and long-term health effects. HSRB State of Knowledge Much is known about the basic nutrition required to maintain performance and health during spaceflight. Standards/controls exist to maintain food safety during spaceflight. Ground data indicates that dehydration and "quicker than usual" weight loss in physically fit individuals will impact cognition and performance. Adequate nutrition and safe food have been demonstrated for 6-month missions and limited 1-year missions that have resupply. Optimizing food/nutrient intake will likely benefit multiple systems, will drive nutrient requirement definitions, and food provisions. There is an uncharacterized risk during LO and LOS missions due to resource restrictions and increased EVAs resulting in reduced food provisioning and preparation capability compared to ISS. The capability to provide safe pre-packaged food with a 5-year shelf life that provides adequate nutrition content, acceptability, safety and variety is a gap. Some countermeasures (CMs) being investigated are: Bioregenerative supplementation and alternative processing, packaging and storage. The impact of both the current and proposed exploration food systems on cognition, performance, behavior, and many other aspects of health is not adequately understood. Potential health impacts include 1) reductions in crew performance (loss of endurance, cognition); 2) crew illness (loss of bone and muscle mass, immune function, cardiovascular performance, gastrointestinal function, severe dehydration, nausea, diarrhea, endocrine function, ocular, psychological health, and the ability to mitigate oxidative damage); 3) long term health effects (cancer, bone, cardio, etc.), 4) interactions with other systems/countermeasures (e.g., drug/nutrient interactions, environment influences on oxidative stress, exercise-induced alterations in energy reqs.). Mitigation Strategy To develop requirements for a nutritious, acceptable/palatable, and safe food system that in addition to providing sustenance can act as a physiological and psychological countermeasure while being balanced with resource constraints.
nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Inadequate Food and Nutrition
Keeping astronauts’ bodies and minds healthy during space flight requires adequate nutrition . Designing meals for a lengthy mission, however, is a complex undertaking. Scientists need to ensure meals are acceptable, safe, nutritious, long-lasting, easy to prepare, and varied enough to avoid menu fatigue . At the International Space Station, resupply shipments include a small portion of fresh fruits and vegetables, alongside limited shelf-life options like pizza kits. Providing desired foods and extending their shelf-life will become even more complex with longer-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, since food must last longer and be optimized for mass and volume, all without regular resupply shipments.
Significant strides have been made toward improving the space food system over the years, like reducing the sodium content and adding new foods for variety. In preparation for a trip to the Red Planet, NASA researchers are focused on enhancing diets to boost nutritional value, designing a space food system that will meet the needs of a long-duration mission, and testing the food system in long-duration analogs and spaceflight.
Astronauts work with scientists to evaluate and select their preferred foods before their mission. Crew members sample menu items, such as soups, meats, and vegetables. More than 200 foods and beverages are available aboard the space station.
Formal risk description: Risk of performance decrement and crew illness due to inadequate food and nutrition

full_title: Risk of Ineffective or Toxic Medications During Long-Duration Exploration Spaceflight
risk_statement: Given that there is no current method to sufficiently characterize medication use, drug quality and performance, clinical outcomes, and the impact of a hostile space environment on pharmaceutical stability and potency during long-duration exploration missions, there is a possibility that provision of a safe and effective drug treatment will be significantly limited, impacting crew health and performance. HSRB State of Knowledge FDA standards followed for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) – require frequent up mass (yearly), which will be problematic for some long duration missions and impossible for Mars Preparatory and Planetary DRMs. Effects of spaceflight environmental conditions on medication stability for long-duration and deep space missions are not fully characterized. It is unclear of how, and to what extent, the spaceflight environment and resultant alterations of human physiology may affect drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. The potential for drug instability compounded by altered drug response poses a significant risk to exploration crews. Additionally, engineering has concerns about medication/suit compatibility. This affects what medications can be administered to the crew in suited operations. The Human Research Program Element (ExMC) research efforts are underway to propose a safe and effective exploration spaceflight formulary able to maintain a ≥ 3 year shelf-life. The proposed ExMC strategy will provide validation for the chemical / physical pharmaceutical stability, degradation product toxicity, and drug safety profiles, and better characterize pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacotherapeutic properties of drugs in the exploration spaceflight environment. Mitigation Strategy NASA’s current Low Earth Orbit (LEO) operations involve frequent resupply missions that may be problematic for some long duration missions and impossible for deep space exploration missions. As such, ensuring a safe and effective pharmacy for exploration missions is an important challenge. At this time, it is unclear how, and to what extent, 1) the spaceflight environment changes drug stability and 2) alterations of human physiology or the medications themselves affect drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. The potential for drug instability compounded by altered drug response may pose a risk to exploration crews. Current research efforts are underway to propose a safe and effective exploration spaceflight formulary able to maintain a ≥ 3 year shelf-life. The proposed ExMC research includes: analysis of medication packaging and storage solutions; studies that will provide validation for chemical / physical pharmaceutical stability; degradation product toxicity and drug safety profiles; and better characterize pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacotherapeutic properties of medications in spaceflight.

full_title: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes
risk_statement: Given exposure to the spaceflight environment can contribute to cardiovascular deconditioning, dysfunction, and remodeling, there is a possibility that crews will experience impaired performance and adverse cardiovascular health outcomes that necessitate intervention during and after spaceflight and planetary operations. HSRB State of Knowledge Exposure to weightlessness and the resulting headward fluid shift alters blood volume, flow, and pressure, manifesting in changes in vascular and cardiac structure and function (e.g., cardiovascular deconditioning, orthostatic intolerance, decreased exercise capacity). In-mission countermeasures and monitoring have been implemented, and available evidence from current missions in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) suggest that functional impairments recover in the weeks/months after landing with a reconditioning program. Less is known following missions >1 year, and there is minimal experience with missions beyond LEO (>14 days) or in partial gravity (>3 days). Epidemiological evidence does not support an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease death in astronauts, but mission durations have been limited largely to 4-6 months and there has been limited follow-up. A statistical increase in atherosclerosis-related cardiovascular pathologies are observed at late time points when exposed to ionizing radiation (e.g., gamma-rays and x-rays) at and above 500 milligray (mGy) terrestrially in human. 2018 National Council on Radiation Protection (NCRP) guidance states “there is not sufficient evidence that absorbed doses in the heart ≤0.5 Gy cause CVDs” (in the context of terrestrial radiation protection) and that the underlying mechanisms are still unclear which makes modeling these effects difficult. Age, sleep, exercise, diet, and stress are known contributors to cardiovascular disease. Resource limitations will affect medical capability and clinical outcomes in mission, particularly in missions at a greater distance from Earth. Mitigation Strategy The strategy for understanding and mitigating spaceflight-induced cardiovascular effects is stepwise and includes: 1) Characterization of the effects of long duration weightlessness and radiation exposure, separately and in combination, through experimentation/research and occupational health monitorin g, 2) development , testing and validation of countermeasures in ground, analog, and low-Earth orbit tests, and finally 3) countermeasure validation in the deep spaceflight environment (Gateway and Artemis). To characterize and understand the effects of each spaceflight hazard (altered gravity, radiation, isolation and confinement, hostile closed environment, and distance from Earth) alone and in combination, ground-based analogs, animal models, and human subjects testing will be used (e.g., bed rest, hindlimb suspension, parabolic flight), as well as long-duration spaceflight opportunities to study cells, tissues, animals, and humans exposed to the conditions of LEO. Because experimental radiation studies are generally limited to in-vitro and animal models, the effects of space radiation (thresholds, dose-responses and the effects of chronic or protracted dose-rates) in isolation and in combination with other spaceflight hazards will be characterized using: 1) long-term astronaut occupational surveillance, 2) by leveraging data from human radiotherapy patients and previously flown astronauts of various durations, and 3) by using current and developing new animal, cell culture, and organ-on-a-chip models for ground-based laboratory studies using space radiation analogs (e.g. NSRL). Additionally, monitoring of astronauts during and after Artemis missions also will be conducted. An emerging medical concern is thrombosis during spaceflight, particularly in the internal jugular vein. Though only one case has been documented, it does not preclude that there have been previous cases that were undetected. Characterization of the incidence of thrombosis and definition of the contributing factors that result in a venous thrombus are high priorities. Confirmation or revision of current preflight screening practices, surveillance activities, and interventions as well as development of countermeasures are of great importance to crew health and mission success, particularly for crewed missions beyond Earth orbit. Countermeasures against orthostatic intolerance (OI) are used operationally to protect crew upon return to Earth, but whether countermeasures are required to protect the crew during head-to-foot accelerations experienced during descent to and ascent from an extraterrestrial surface is not defined. An investigation of OI in males and females with and without lower body compression garments during varying simulated gravity levels is ongoing . The results of this study will help inform the standards and requirements defining the acceleration limits for the Human Landing System Program with and without compression garment and whether additional OI countermeasures may be needed. Candidate c ountermeasure identification and development for non-orthostatic intolerance concerns rely upon data mining, monitoring emerging research and developments highlighted at conferences, literature review, the NASA process of Request for Information (RFI), studies using human iPSCs (human-induced pluripotent stem cell), and workshops and technical interchange meetings (TIM) with key experts. Countermeasure testing will be conducted on the ground in established animal models and human subject-relevant spaceflight analogs followed by demonstration of countermeasure efficacy in ISS astronauts. Data collection on astronauts during and after Artemis missions using the suggested countermeasures will complete the mitigation strategy.
nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations
Low-gravity conditions and other spaceflight stressors can alter the heart and blood vessels , potentially leading to blood clots, heart arrythmias, cardiovascular disease, and low blood pressure which elevates the chances of fainting at landing. The risk of developing these conditions will increase with longer-duration missions such as a multi-year trip to Mars, so research focused on understanding and treating these risks is a priority for NASA.
Regular exercise and healthy diets help crews maintain cardiovascular fitness. Lower-body compression garments and drinking lots of fluids prior to landing can help to prevent low blood pressure. For future Mars missions, astronauts will also receive enhanced training to respond to cardiovascular emergencies.
Low gravity can also physically change the shape of the human heart , making it become more spherical.

full_title: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
risk_statement: Given that exposure to a reduced gravity environment causes cardio-respiratory (e.g., maximal oxygen consumption and ventilatory threshold) and musculoskeletal fitness (e.g., strength, power, and endurance) to decline, there is a risk of impaired mission task performance and adverse health outcomes. Note: This risk is carried as two separate risks at the HSRB. The content in this field has been developed by HRP. HSRB State of Knowledge Despite the use of inflight exercise countermeasures on the International Space Station (ISS), current evidence suggests that cardio-respiratory and musculoskeletal fitness decrease during spaceflight and after spaceflight, though individual variability is evident that cannot be fully explained by countermeasure adherence. During ISS missions, some astronauts do not meet the current fitness standards for operations in weightlessness, and many astronauts would not meet current fitness standards for extravehicular operations on celestial surfaces. Further, many have not returned to preflight fitness levels by the end of the standard reconditioning program (30 days after landing). Limited data exist for astronauts who participate in spaceflight missions greater than the standard ISS mission duration (4-6 months), for women astronauts, and during and after partial gravity exposures. In long-duration missions on ISS, astronauts have access for a robust suite of exercise countermeasures (cycle ergometer, treadmill, resistive exercise) but countermeasure capabilities likely will be reduced for exploration missions due to mass, volume, and power limitations. As the design and architecture of future exploration missions evolve (e.g., vehicle design, spacesuit design, mission objectives), characterization of physical requirements to perform critical tasks and of crew health in these novel mission scenarios is required to inform and refine the requirements for countermeasures against cardio-respiratory and musculoskeletal deconditioning and the physical fitness standards which these countermeasures are intended to support. Note: This risk is carried as two separate risks at the HSRB. The content in this field has been developed by HRP. Mitigation Strategy Extended duration spaceflight mission studies and evaluations of novel exercise systems on ISS, Orion, and Gateway as well as in spaceflight or ground analogs are planned to help inform this risk for exploration class missions, including Mars mission parameters. EVA task-specific evaluations will include assessment of the fitness levels required to successfully perform mission tasks. This includes measuring metabolic costs and muscle strength requirements of critical tasks and of individual factors contributing to task success (e.g., anthropometry, hydration and caloric intake, fatigue, and sex). Operational Relevance: If muscle and/or cardio-respiratory fitness are below levels required to perform mission critical tasks then the crew are at higher risks for compromised performance capabilities. The compromised capabilities could impact the ability to complete mission objectives and result in decreased mission efficiency and efficacy, or increased risk for injury or other health impacts. Programs need to provide adequate exercise systems and time to perform the exercise to maintain performance capabilities across all phases of the mission (pre-, in-, and post-flight). HRP needs to provide the SME knowledge and contribute to the data needs to develop programmatic exercise system requirements.
nasa_ref_summary:
Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
Living in microgravity can weaken the bones, muscles, and cardiopulmonary systems of astronauts, making it difficult for them to carry out critical mission tasks while also increasing the risk of injury. These physiological changes can make falling or tripping more likely, especially during gravitational transitions to the surface of the Moon or Mars, or when returning to their daily living on Earth.
Six to seven days a week, astronauts on the International Space Station perform resistance training and aerobic exercises for 1.5 hours per day to maintain their fitness and protect against muscle and bone loss. Crew members also undergo periodic fitness self-evaluations to help researchers monitor their health and fitness and to optimize the astronauts’ training regimen. Spacecraft set to carry astronauts to the Moon and Mars, however, will likely have less space for exercise equipment. Consequently, researchers are working to understand how to optimize both exercise machines and protocols to ensure that astronaut health is maintained on these deep space missions.
The effects of exposure to microgravity can vary substantially between individual astronauts. However, data from International Space Station missions indicates that average losses to strength and aerobic fitness are 10-12% of pre-mission levels. Depending on how it’s measured, between 12-38% of space station crew members lose more than 20% of their pre-mission fitness. Strength loss affects a larger proportion of crew members than does the decline in aerobic fitness. Losses are seen across physical performance areas, including upper and lower body strength and endurance, flexibility, aerobic fitness, agility, and coordination.
